instructions: Put the hijiki in a bowl, cover it with 4 cups of cold water, and leave it for 10 minutes.
Meanwhile, put the aburaage in a bowl and pour boiling water over it to rinse off the oil. Squeeze it dry, cut it in half lengthwise, and slice it thin.
Cut the carrot into thin matchsticks. Stir the dashi powder into 2 cups of hot water until it dissolves.
Drain the hijiki and rinse it under running water. Drain it well.
Heat the oil in a medium pot over medium heat. Add the carrot and cook for 2 minutes, stirring, until it's coated and slightly soft.
Add the hijiki and aburaage and stir for 1 minute.
Pour in the dashi and bring to a boil. Add the mirin, sugar and soy sauce, then reduce to medium-low, cover, and cook for 20 minutes.
Add the edamame. Cook uncovered for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until most of the liquid has cooked away and you can see the bottom of the pot when you drag a spoon through.
Take the pot off the heat and stir in the sesame seeds.
Serve it at room temperature or cold. Store it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 4 days, or freeze for up to 1 month.
method_notes: Just One Cookbook leads (4.87 from 43). Hijiki is soaked, sautéed with carrot and fried tofu, then simmered in dashi, mirin, sugar and soy sauce until the liquid is gone, and eaten at room temperature. Onolicious Hawaii (4.5 from 11) is nearly the same and finishes with sesame seeds, which is where the seeds come from. The lotus root and konnyaku are left out, and a vegan dashi powder stands in for the dashi. The list's description says a sesame-soy dressing, but every version read is a simmered salad. It keeps well, which is why it suits a packed lunch.
